title: What Can Student-AI Dialogues Tell Us About Students’ Self-Regulated Learning? An exploratory framework
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether student-AI dialogue logs can serve as a valid, non-interruptive source for assessing students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) in Human-AI Collaborative Learning environments. The authors argue that conventional SRL measures are increasingly inadequate in dialogue-centric learning settings: questionnaires interrupt learning and capture only general perceptions, while clickstream data becomes less informative when much of the learning activity occurs inside a conversational AI interface. The study therefore asks what dialogue patterns emerge in student-GenAI interactions, which of those patterns are associated with stronger or weaker SRL, and whether dialogue behavior differs between high- and low-SRL students.

To investigate this, the researchers collected 421 dialogue logs from students using a bespoke HAICL system supported by Doubao v1.6, and measured SRL using the Online Self-Regulated Learning Questionnaire (OSLQ). Using large language model embeddings and clustering, they identified 22 dialogue patterns spanning pre-class and post-class student questions and AI responses. They then computed alignment scores for each student across these patterns and analyzed associations with overall SRL and its subdimensions using Spearman correlations, followed by Mann-Whitney U tests comparing high- and low-SRL groups.

The study involved second-year undergraduate finance students enrolled in a mandatory introductory statistics course at a single university. The activity took place over four weeks during the middle of the semester. Students used the AI system weekly for two purposes: pre-class preparation and post-class review/planning. Before the study, participants received training on how to use the HAICL system. At the end of the period, they submitted complete AI dialogue logs and then completed the OSLQ. After excluding students who did not complete the questionnaire, analyses were based on 98 students.

The main conclusion is that student-AI dialogues contain meaningful behavioral indicators of SRL. Proactive dialogue patterns such as post-class systematic knowledge integration were positively associated with stronger SRL, while reactive patterns such as foundational conceptual difficulties and AI responses involving heavy scaffolding were negatively associated with SRL. Low-SRL students showed greater alignment with these reactive patterns than high-SRL students. Based on these findings, the authors propose the Dialogue-Based Human-AI Self-Regulated Learning (DHASRL) framework, intended to support real-time monitoring and scaffolding of SRL in AI-supported learning environments.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI learning partner used within a bespoke Human-AI Collaborative Learning (HAICL) system to support dialogue-based learning interactions.
identified_tools.use_case: University students in an introductory statistics course used a bespoke HAICL system supported by doubao v1.6 for pre-class preparation and post-class review; the study analyzed student-AI dialogue logs to infer self-regulated learning (SRL) patterns and proposed the DHASRL framework for real-time SRL monitoring/scaffolding.

findings.finding_summary: In 421 dialogue logs from 98 university students, several dialogue patterns were significantly associated with overall SRL and its subdimensions on the OSLQ. Proactive post-class systematic knowledge integration (PostQ_cluster5) was positively associated with overall SRL (r = .164) and goal setting (r = .293), whereas reactive/foundational and scaffolding-intensive patterns such as PreQ_cluster1 (r = -.190), PreR_cluster1 (r = -.191), PostR_cluster4 (r = -.220), and PostR_cluster5 (r = -.230) were negatively associated with overall SRL.
findings.measure: Online Self-Regulated Learning Questionnaire (OSLQ) total and subscale scores correlated with 22 dialogue pattern alignment scores

findings.finding_summary: Median-split group comparisons showed that low-SRL students aligned significantly more with reactive dialogue patterns than high-SRL students. Specifically, the low-SRL group showed higher means for PreQ_cluster1 (.555 vs .520, p = .009), PostQ_cluster0 (.549 vs .525, p = .042), PreR_cluster0 (.608 vs .583, p = .042), PreR_cluster1 (.527 vs .495, p = .006), PostR_cluster2 (.603 vs .575, p = .029), PostR_cluster3 (.595 vs .570, p = .031), and PostR_cluster5 (.598 vs .559, p = .004).
findings.measure: Mann-Whitney U comparisons of dialogue pattern alignment scores between high- and low-SRL groups

quality_tier_rationale: This is an observational correlational study using dialogue logs and questionnaire scores, not a randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation of an intervention's causal effects. The analyses are systematic and include FDR correction, but the evidence remains associational.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported associations with SRL are statistically significant but generally small in magnitude (roughly r=.13 to .29 in the positive direction, with several negative correlations). The paper demonstrates promising diagnostic utility for SRL tracing, but impact on learning outcomes is unclear and not causally tested.
